parts.label: a.i
parts.display_text: A 6.8 × 10⁴ kg spacecraft enters a circular orbit 300 km above Earth. Use Earth mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.4 × 10⁶ m. Calculate its increase in gravitational potential energy from the surface.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: a.ii
parts.display_text: For the same spacecraft and Earth data, calculate the circular-orbit speed at altitude 300 km.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: a.iii
parts.display_text: Estimate the mechanical energy required to put a 6.8 × 10⁴ kg spacecraft into this orbit from rest on Earth’s surface, ignoring Earth’s rotation and losses.

answer.text: The gain is GMm(1/R − 1/(2r)) ≈ 2.2 × 10¹² J. This includes both the potential-energy increase and the final orbital kinetic energy.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.given_text: Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹, M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg, R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m and orbital radius r = 6.7 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: b
parts.display_text: Explain why astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft feel weightless even though Earth exerts a gravitational force on them.

answer.text: The astronauts and spacecraft fall freely with essentially the same gravitational acceleration. No supporting normal force is needed; apparent weight is zero although gravity is not.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: c-gravity
parts.display_text: Treat a spacecraft of mass 6.8 × 10⁴ kg as a point mass. Estimate its gravitational field strength 10 m from its centre.

parts.label: c-time
parts.display_text: In a simplified model, an object starts from rest 2.0 m from a surface and accelerates toward it at a constant 4.5 × 10⁻⁸ m s⁻². Estimate the travel time.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

duplicate-38b702f4f863e7c2.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q32:whole.hint: Compare the starting total mechanical energy with the minimum needed to reach infinity.
notes: With zero potential at infinity, the minimum escape condition is ½mv_e² − GMm/R = 0, so v_e = √(2GM/R).
Escape speed is different from circular orbital speed at the same radius. For ratios, use √(M/R); the escaping object’s mass cancels.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q33:whole.hint: Distinguish energy per kilogram from the energy of the whole object.
notes: With zero at infinity, gravitational potential is V_g = −GM/r and potential energy is mV_g. Work required for a slow move is m(V_final − V_initial).
Potential is a scalar, so add its contributions algebraically. Use mgΔh only for a small height change where g is approximately uniform.

Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q19:c-gravity.hint: Draw the direction towards each attracting mass and measure distances from the centres of the masses.
notes: Outside a spherical mass, g = GM/r² and F = mg. Add field contributions as vectors when more than one mass is present.
An altitude above a surface is not the radius in the formula: r = R + h. The test mass affects force but not the field strength at its position.

kirk-17476a9c55b97386-q19:c-time.hint: Draw the velocities with their reference frames labelled. Which two vectors combine to give the required motion?
notes: At non-relativistic speeds, v(A relative to C) = v(A relative to B) + v(B relative to C). Resolve perpendicular directions separately.
For a magnitude and direction, combine the components using Pythagoras and a labelled angle. Do not add the magnitudes of perpendicular velocities.
“From rest” sets the initial velocity to zero. It does not say that the acceleration is zero.

Nuclear radius scales approximately as A^(1/3), giving roughly constant nuclear density. Outer electrons control chemical behaviour; the nucleus controls radioactive properties.

Subtract background from measured count rates before finding a decay ratio. Activity counts decays per second; it is not the total number of undecayed nuclei.
